<explanation>
Based on our deep dive into the Perses repository and README, the system is a full‐stack observability dashboard tool designed not only to visualize Prometheus metrics and Tempo traces but also to serve as an extensible “dashboard-as-code” platform with native CLI tools, SDKs (both Go and Cuelang), plugin integrations, and GitOps-friendly automation. Here’s how you can create an accurate and detailed system design diagram for Perses:

1. Identify the Major Components
   • Backend API Server: This is the core service implemented in Go. In the file tree you’ll notice extensive code in directories like “internal/api”, “cmd/perses”, “pkg”, and “internal/cli”. This endpoint handles RESTful operations for dashboards, datasources, authentication/authorization, and more.
   • Frontend UI: The “ui” folder (and its subfolders like “ui/dashboards”, “ui/explore”, “ui/plugin-system”, “ui/core”) is a React-based web application. It provides the interactive experience for building, editing, and exploring dashboards.
   • CLI & SDK Tools: There are CLI components (located under “cmd/percli” and “internal/cli”) and SDKs (see “go-sdk” and “cue”) that let users programmatically manage dashboard definitions, making Perses “dashboard-as-code” and GitOps-friendly.
   • Plugin Architecture: Perses is built to be extensible, with directories like “internal/api/plugin”, “scripts/plugin”, and “ui/plugin-system” outlining how additional functionalities (such as new panel types) can be integrated.
   • External Integrations: The system is designed to integrate external observability tools (like Prometheus and Tempo) as data sources for metrics and traces. Draw a connection or “data-edge” in your diagram to represent these external services.
   • Configuration and Validation via Cuelang: The “cue” directory shows that Perses uses Cuelang for defining dashboard specifications and validations, contributing to its flexible dashboard-as-code approach.

2. Representing Relationships and Interactions
   • Draw a layered diagram where the Frontend (React UI) communicates via API calls (typically HTTP/REST) to the Backend API Server.
   • Depict the CLI tools and SDKs as separate clients that interact with the API Server for provisioning, migration, and GitOps operations.
   • Show the Plugin System as either a separate module or as an integrated part of both front- and back-end components, indicating that plugins can be loaded externally to extend functionalities.
   • Highlight connections to external services (Prometheus, Tempo) using directional arrows coming into the Backend API (or sometimes directly queried by the UI) for fetching telemetry data.
   • Indicate that configuration files (e.g., in the “cue” directory) feed into the dashboard creation pipelines and are used by the backend for validation and migration logic.

3. Emphasize Architectural Patterns
   • MVC / Layered Architecture: The backend organizes request processing via controllers/endpoints, middleware (e.g., authentication, error handling), and persistence layers (databases or file-based storage).
   • Modular and Plugin-Oriented Design: Both for frontend and backend, show how the plugin architecture allows for extensibility.
   • GitOps and Dashboard-as-Code: Include a note that Perses embraces a dashboard-as-code approach, meaning that dashboards, configurations, and even plugins can be managed via version control systems and automated CI/CD pipelines.

4. Include Relevant Technologies and Frameworks
   • Backend: Go (with various internal API modules, middleware, database access, authentication modules, and proxy capabilities).
   • Frontend: React (with a rich component library spread across multiple UI sub-projects such as “ui/app”, “ui/dashboards”, and “ui/plugin-system”).
   • CLI Tools: Built in Go for interacting with the backend API and facilitating GitOps workflows.
   • Cuelang for dashboard specification and validation.
   • External Observability: Integration points for Prometheus (metrics) and Tempo (traces).

5. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines
   • For this full-stack application, clearly separate distinct tiers: the frontend UI layer; the backend server (with its API endpoints, middleware, and plugin management); and external integrators (e.g., Prometheus/Tempo).
   • For GitOps and dashboard-as-code aspects, include a side panel for configuration management that interacts with CLI tools and SDKs.
   • Add a “Plugin” component that shows both build-time (in CLI/scripts) and runtime (in UI and API) integrations.

6. Diagram Elements and Visual Details
   • Use clear, descriptive labels for each component: “Perses API Server”, “React UI (Dashboard Frontend)”, “CLI & SDK Clients”, “Plugin Manager”, “External Data Sources (Prometheus, Tempo)”, etc.
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate the flow of data: for example, from the frontend ➜ API server; from the CLI/SDK ➜ API server; and from external data sources ➜ API server.
   • Apply color coding or different shapes to distinguish between types of components (e.g., rectangles for servers, cylinders for external databases/services, and icons or ovals for command-line tools).
   • Make sure to annotate connections with protocols or design patterns (e.g., “REST API”, “configuration via Cuelang”, “plugin extension interface”).

Following these guidelines will ensure that your system design diagram comprehensively reflects the architecture of Perses. You’ll capture core components, their interactions, and extensibility points, all aligned with its use cases as a dashboard tool that integrates observability data, supports GitOps, and enables dashboard-as-code workflows.
</explanation>
